turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Number 149, you say? A rather large house, I presume? One requires space, you know, for adequate entertaining and the proper display of one's position in society.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mama, must you interrogate him so? I've already told you, I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, and I expect a certain amount of consideration for my happiness!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Consideration for *your* happiness, my dear, is directly proportional to my assessment of the gentleman who inspires it. Let us return, then, to Mr. Worthing—a large house, you say? One hopes it is suitably furnished, and not, I trust, overrun with… servants.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Servants are quite dreadful, Mama, but surely that is *his* concern, not mine! I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, and I simply cannot bear this relentless inquisition any longer.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: My dear Gwendolen, your happiness is of the utmost importance, naturally, but it cannot be allowed to eclipse the fundamental principles of propriety. Servants, you say, are dreadful? One might well agree, but their presence, or lack thereof, speaks volumes about a gentleman’s understanding of his responsibilities. Now, Mr. Worthing, pray tell me, do you employ a butler?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: A butler, Lady Bracknell? Yes, of course, I have a butler. He's… quite efficient, I assure you, though I confess I don't often concern myself with the specifics of his duties.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Efficiency, Mr. Worthing, is a virtue, but it does not compensate for a deficiency in breeding. A butler's efficiency is, after all, entirely dependent upon the quality of his master's judgment in selecting him. Pray, tell me, how did you *acquire* this…efficient butler?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He was… recommended, Lady Bracknell. By a… a mutual acquaintance, you see. I wouldn’t presume to know the particulars of his previous employment, but I’m certain he’s a man of impeccable discretion.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A mutual acquaintance, you say? How exceedingly vague! I find a lack of specificity deeply unsettling, Mr. Worthing. One must know the provenance of everything, particularly when it concerns one’s servants; it is a matter of vital importance to the preservation of good order.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: A mutual acquaintance, yes, quite right. It was… a family friend, Lady Bracknell, a gentleman of considerable standing, who assured me of his capabilities. I wouldn't wish to trouble you with the details, as I'm sure they’re rather… commonplace.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A family friend, you say? How very convenient. I trust this 'family friend' possesses unimpeachable lineage, Mr. Worthing? One cannot be too cautious when entrusting matters of such consequence to intermediaries.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell, my family friend is a gentleman of excellent repute. I believe his name is…well, it escapes me at the moment, but I assure you he comes from a very respectable family, though perhaps not as… as widely known as your own, of course.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: “'It escapes you at the moment,' you say? Mr. Worthing, I find that a most distressing admission! A gentleman should possess the names of his associates with the same diligence he applies to the ordering of his cuff buttons. It speaks volumes, you see, volumes!” ,

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mama, must you interrogate Mr. Worthing so? I've already declared my engagement, and I’m quite certain he’s perfectly satisfactory; I wouldn’t have chosen him otherwise.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Gwendolen, my dear, your impetuosity is charming, but hardly a substitute for due consideration! A declaration, however ardent, does not absolve one from the necessity of proper scrutiny. I am merely attempting to ascertain whether this gentleman possesses the requisite qualities to uphold the dignity of our name.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Forgive me, Lady Bracknell, my memory isn't always what it should be. I'm certain I can recall the name presently, if you'll permit me a moment… it’s quite possible I’m simply a little flustered by the…the gravity of the occasion.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A moment, Mr. Worthing? A moment is precisely what one requires to unravel the tangled threads of a gentleman’s memory! I trust this temporary lapse is not indicative of a more pervasive intellectual deficiency?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Oh dear, no, Lady Bracknell, I assure you it's nothing of the sort! I simply… I travel quite a bit, you see, and one doesn’t always keep track of every acquaintance. I'm perfectly capable, I promise!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Travelling, you say? A most convenient explanation, Mr. Worthing, for a regrettable lack of rootedness. One expects a gentleman of prospects to possess a certain… stability, a connection to family and place, not merely a penchant for transient encounters!

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell, you are quite right. I do have… well, I *am* rather fond of travelling, yes, but I assure you I have every intention of establishing myself properly, should… should I be fortunate enough to secure the… the favour of Miss Fairfax and her family. It’s just that… well, I find the world a rather fascinating place!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
